title: Uruk, the first big city
blurb: By about 3300 BCE, Uruk in southern Mesopotamia had grown into something new: a city of tens of thousands of people, most of whom did not grow their own food. It had huge temple buildings, mass-produced pottery, and officials who kept track of grain, sheep and labour. Its goods and styles turn up from Iran to Syria and Anatolia.

title: Writing begins as bookkeeping
blurb: The first writing was accounting. Around 3300 BCE, Uruk's administrators pressed signs into clay tablets to record grain, beer, cloth and livestock. Over the next centuries the signs came to stand for sounds, so they could record names, laws, letters and stories. Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared at almost the same time. Writing was later invented from scratch in China and in Mesoamerica.
dateNote: The oldest tablets from Uruk are dated to roughly 3350 to 3200 BCE.

title: Herders from the steppe
blurb: Around 3300 BCE the Yamnaya herders appeared on the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas, and by 3000 BCE they ranged from Hungary to Kazakhstan. About 4,500 years ago, people in central Europe traced roughly three-quarters of their ancestry to them. Ancient DNA suggests these migrations carried at least some of Europe's Indo-European languages, though where that language family first arose is still argued over.
debate: Where and when the Indo-European languages began. Ancient DNA supports a spread from the steppe into Europe; a 2023 study of vocabulary dates the family's root to about 8,100 years ago, earlier than the steppe migrations.
dateNote: The Yamnaya culture appeared around 3300 BCE. This stop starts at 3000 BCE, when it reached its widest extent.

title: The planned cities of the Indus
blurb: From about 2600 BCE, cities rose along the Indus and neighbouring rivers in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out in an orderly plan, with baked-brick houses, wells, bathing rooms and covered drains. Their people traded by sea with Mesopotamia and used a script nobody has deciphered. After about 1900 BCE the cities emptied, probably as the monsoon weakened.

title: Caral: cities on the far side of the world
blurb: While pyramids were rising in Egypt, people on the desert coast of Peru were raising their own. Caral, occupied from about 2600 to 2000 BCE, had six large platform mounds and sunken circular plazas, fed by irrigated fields. Its builders had no pottery and no writing, and no contact with any other city-builders. Cities were invented more than once.

title: The Great Pyramid, and the last mammoths
blurb: Around 2560 BCE, Egypt's king Khufu had the Great Pyramid built at Giza. Papyrus logbooks found at a Red Sea harbour, the oldest inscribed papyri known, record a work crew ferrying limestone blocks to the site. Far to the north, a small herd of woolly mammoths was still alive on Wrangel Island in the Arctic. They died out about 4,000 years ago.

title: Kerma, a Nubian kingdom on the Nile
blurb: Around 2500 BCE, at the northern end of the Great Bend of the Nile in what is now Sudan, Nubians founded Kerma, the earliest city in Africa outside Egypt. Its kings came to rule much of the Nile valley south of Egypt and were buried in vast tombs with hundreds of sacrifices. Kerma traded and fought with Egypt for centuries, until Egyptian armies conquered it around 1450 BCE.

title: The first empire, and the first author we can name
blurb: Around 2340 BCE Sargon of Akkad conquered the city-states of Sumer and joined peoples of different languages and gods under one ruler: the first empire. He made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess of the moon god at Ur. She wrote hymns in Sumerian and named herself in them, "I, Enheduanna", which makes her the earliest author we know by name.

title: Hammurabi's laws in stone
blurb: Hammurabi, king of Babylon from 1792 to 1750 BCE, had his laws carved on a basalt pillar more than two metres tall, topped by a relief of the king before the sun god Shamash. He wrote that they were meant so "the strong should not harm the weak". Punishments depended on rank: putting out a man's eye cost an eye, but a slave's eye cost half the slave's value.

title: Lapita voyagers sail into the open Pacific
blurb: Between about 1500 and 1300 BCE a new style of pottery, called Lapita, appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea. Within two or three centuries its makers sailed east into the open Pacific, reaching Vanuatu, then Fiji, then Tonga around 890 BCE, islands where no one had lived before. Ancient DNA shows that the first settlers of Vanuatu had little or no Papuan ancestry.

title: Bronze, tin and the Uluburun ship
blurb: Around 1320 BCE a merchant ship sank off Uluburun on the coast of Turkey. It carried 10 tonnes of copper ingots from Cyprus and a tonne of tin, the two metals that make bronze. Tin is far rarer than copper. Chemical tests show that a third of the ship's tin came from ores in today's Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and the rest from Turkey's Taurus Mountains.

title: Shang China and the oracle bones
blurb: The oldest Chinese writing known is carved on oracle bones: ox shoulder blades and turtle shells used for divination by the kings of the late Shang dynasty. Over 150,000 have been found, most at Yinxu near Anyang, the late Shang capital. Until 1899 farmers sold them as "dragon bones" for medicine. Radiocarbon dates put King Wu Ding's reign at about 1254 to 1197 BCE.
dateNote: The dates span the late Shang, from Wu Ding's reign to the dynasty's end around 1041 BCE, as estimated from radiocarbon dates on the bones.

title: The Bronze Age world falls apart
blurb: Within about fifty years of 1200 BCE, the connected world of the eastern Mediterranean came apart. The Hittite empire vanished, the Mycenaean palaces burned, the trading city of Ugarit was destroyed and never rebuilt, and Egypt lost its lands abroad. Historians point to drought, earthquakes, migration and war, and to how much these states had come to depend on one another.
debate: No single cause is agreed. Knapp and Manning argue for many local crises over decades; others give more weight to a long drought.
